category: Adjectives that change meaning after the noun

examples: The present owners bought the house in 2015.
We can't hire anyone in the present economy.
The present system just isn't working.
Everyone present voted for the plan.
Were you present at the meeting on Monday?
A parent must be present during the interview.
Traces of lead were present in the drinking water.
The virus may be present in the blood for weeks.
Racism is still present in many parts of society.
The present study looks at teenagers in rural Ohio.
In the present case, the court found no evidence of fraud.
Put your phone away and be present with your kids.
She tries to stay present instead of worrying about next week.
I want to be more present with my family.
She goes is in the present tense; she went is in the past.
The present participle always ends in -ing.

senses.head: Existing or happening now; current — before the noun
examples: The present owners bought the house in 2015.
We can't hire anyone in the present economy.
The present system just isn't working.

senses.head: In a particular place or at an event; there — after the noun or after a verb
examples: Everyone present voted for the plan.
Were you present at the meeting on Monday?
A parent must be present during the interview.

senses.head: Existing or found in something, such as a substance, a place or a group
examples: Traces of lead were present in the drinking water.
The virus may be present in the blood for weeks.
Racism is still present in many parts of society.

senses.head: Being dealt with or discussed now; this one — formal, before the noun
examples: The present study looks at teenagers in rural Ohio.
In the present case, the court found no evidence of fraud.

senses.head: Giving your full attention to what is happening now, not distracted
examples: Put your phone away and be present with your kids.
She tries to stay present instead of worrying about next week.
I want to be more present with my family.

senses.head: In grammar, expressing the time now — in present tense, present participle
examples: She goes is in the present tense; she went is in the past.
The present participle always ends in -ing.

entries.position: both — before a noun = current (the present owner); after the noun or after be = in attendance (the people present, Was he present?)
entries.comparison: not gradable — except in the attentive sense: more present
entries.takes: at + event (present at the meeting); in + place or substance = found in (present in the water)
entries.contrast: Position changes the meaning. Before the noun present = current: the present members (нынешние члены). After the noun or after be = in the room: the members present (присутствующие члены), Ten members were present. Russian настоящий in the sense real is real or genuine, not present: a real friend (настоящий друг), not a present friend. The noun a present (подарок) has the same sound; the verb to present is stressed on the second syllable (prih-ZENT). at present (в настоящее время) is a fixed phrase.

examples: Doctors are concerned about the rise in measles cases.
Concerned parents packed the school board meeting.
I'm more concerned about the cost than the time.
The students concerned will be contacted by email.
It was a hard decision for everyone concerned.
Talk to the people who are directly concerned.
The first chapter is concerned with life in 1930s Chicago.
Economics is concerned with how people use limited resources.
He was more concerned with winning than with playing fair.
She's not concerned with what other people think.
As far as I'm concerned, the matter is closed.
As far as money is concerned, we're doing fine.

senses.head: Worried about something or someone
examples: Doctors are concerned about the rise in measles cases.
Concerned parents packed the school board meeting.
I'm more concerned about the cost than the time.

senses.head: Involved in or affected by something — right after the noun, or after be
body: (причастный, имеющий отношение; о котором идёт речь)
examples: The students concerned will be contacted by email.
It was a hard decision for everyone concerned.
Talk to the people who are directly concerned.

senses.head: About a particular subject; dealing with it — in be concerned with
examples: The first chapter is concerned with life in 1930s Chicago.
Economics is concerned with how people use limited resources.

senses.head: Caring about something and thinking it important — in be concerned with
examples: He was more concerned with winning than with playing fair.
She's not concerned with what other people think.

senses.head: In as far as … is concerned: in someone's opinion, or when talking about something
examples: As far as I'm concerned, the matter is closed.
As far as money is concerned, we're doing fine.

entries.position: both — before a noun or after be = worried (a concerned parent, We're concerned); right after the noun = involved, affected (the parents concerned)
entries.comparison: more/most — in the worried sense: more concerned, most concerned
entries.takes: about or for + noun = worried (concerned about the cost, concerned for her safety); with + noun or -ing = dealing with, or caring about (concerned with facts); that-clause = worried that; as far as … is concerned
entries.contrast: Position and preposition change the meaning. Before the noun concerned = worried: a concerned parent (обеспокоенный родитель). Right after the noun = involved: the parent concerned (тот родитель, о котором идёт речь). concerned about/for = worried; concerned with = about a subject, or caring about something: The book is concerned with the Civil War (посвящена). concerning is not the adjective of worry in careful writing: it is a preposition (concerning your letter = о вашем письме); in American speech a concerning trend (тревожная тенденция) is common but informal.

examples: Who's responsible for the kids this weekend?
She's responsible for hiring new staff.
Parents are legally responsible for their children's safety.
Police are still looking for the people responsible.
Smoking is responsible for most cases of lung cancer.
The landlord was held responsible for the damage.
She's a very responsible kid for her age.
My brother is more responsible than I was at sixteen.
The company promotes responsible drinking.
She holds a responsible position at the bank.
It's a very responsible job for someone so young.
The police chief is responsible to the city council.
The inspector general is responsible only to Congress.

senses.head: Having the job or duty of dealing with something, and having to answer for it
examples: Who's responsible for the kids this weekend?
She's responsible for hiring new staff.
Parents are legally responsible for their children's safety.

senses.head: Being the cause of something, especially something bad; to blame
examples: Police are still looking for the people responsible.
Smoking is responsible for most cases of lung cancer.
The landlord was held responsible for the damage.

senses.head: Sensible and able to be trusted to do the right thing, or done in a sensible, careful way
examples: She's a very responsible kid for her age.
My brother is more responsible than I was at sixteen.
The company promotes responsible drinking.

senses.head: Of a job or position: involving important duties and decisions
examples: She holds a responsible position at the bank.
It's a very responsible job for someone so young.

senses.head: Having to report to a person or group that has authority over you — in responsible to
examples: The police chief is responsible to the city council.
The inspector general is responsible only to Congress.

entries.position: both — before a noun = sensible, trustworthy (a responsible adult) or with important duties (a responsible job); right after the noun = the one who caused it or is in charge (the person responsible); after be, any of these (She's responsible for sales, He's very responsible)
entries.takes: for + noun or -ing = in charge of, or the cause of (responsible for the accident); to + person or group = answering to (responsible to the board)
entries.contrast: Position changes the meaning. Before the noun responsible usually = sensible, reliable: a responsible person (ответственный человек). Right after the noun = the one who did it: the person responsible (виновник, тот, кто это сделал). The preposition is for: responsible for the budget, not responsible of or responsible about. responsible to is different: it names the boss you answer to. responsible for can be duty (responsible for sales) or blame (responsible for the accident); context decides. For a job, Americans also often say in charge of: She's in charge of security. Don't confuse with responsive (quick to react: a responsive website).

examples: Everyone involved in the project got a bonus.
Police want to talk to anyone who was involved.
Two cars were involved in the accident.
Do you understand the risks involved?
There's a lot of paperwork involved in adopting a child.
The work involved was more than we expected.
Kids with involved parents tend to do better in school.
She's more involved in the community than anyone I know.
I got so involved in the book that I missed my stop.
Getting a visa is a long, involved process.
The plot is too involved to explain in a few words.
She's involved with someone she met at work.
Were they romantically involved?

senses.head: Taking part in something, or connected with it in some way
examples: Everyone involved in the project got a bonus.
Police want to talk to anyone who was involved.
Two cars were involved in the accident.

senses.head: Needed as a necessary part or result of something — after the noun
examples: Do you understand the risks involved?
There's a lot of paperwork involved in adopting a child.
The work involved was more than we expected.

senses.head: Giving a lot of time, attention and energy to something
examples: Kids with involved parents tend to do better in school.
She's more involved in the community than anyone I know.
I got so involved in the book that I missed my stop.

senses.head: Complicated and having many parts, so hard to follow — usually before the noun
examples: Getting a visa is a long, involved process.
The plot is too involved to explain in a few words.

senses.head: Having a romantic or sexual relationship with someone
examples: She's involved with someone she met at work.
Were they romantically involved?

entries.position: both — before a noun = complicated (a long, involved story) or active, engaged (involved parents); right after the noun = taking part, or needed as part of it (the people involved, the costs involved); after a verb, any of these (She got involved, The process is very involved)
entries.takes: in + noun or -ing = taking part in; with + noun = working closely with, or in a relationship with (involved with a coworker)
entries.contrast: Position changes the meaning. Before the noun involved usually = complicated: an involved explanation (запутанное объяснение); with people it = active, engaged: an involved father (отец, который много занимается детьми). After the noun = taking part or connected: the people involved (участники, причастные), the costs involved (связанные с этим расходы). involved in a thing = taking part in it; involved with a person = working closely with them, or having a romantic relationship. Russian участвовать, вмешиваться often comes out as get involved: I don't want to get involved (не хочу в это ввязываться).

examples: Make sure you use the proper tools.
Put everything back in its proper place.
The form wasn't filled out in the proper way.
I haven't had a proper meal all day.
The town doesn't even have a proper grocery store, just a gas station.
It isn't proper to talk with your mouth full.
Her grandmother was a very proper lady.
He was always more proper than his brothers.
The city proper has about 600,000 people, but the metro area has two million.
We didn't reach the town proper until noon.
The meeting proper doesn't start until ten.
The judge acted within the powers proper to her office.
They studied the plants proper to the desert Southwest.
Chicago is a proper noun, so it starts with a capital letter.
Most proper names don't take the.

senses.head: Right, correct or suitable for the situation or the job
examples: Make sure you use the proper tools.
Put everything back in its proper place.
The form wasn't filled out in the proper way.

senses.head: Real and complete; of the kind it should be
examples: I haven't had a proper meal all day.
The town doesn't even have a proper grocery store, just a gas station.

senses.head: Following the accepted rules of polite or formal behavior
examples: It isn't proper to talk with your mouth full.
Her grandmother was a very proper lady.
He was always more proper than his brothers.

senses.head: In its strict or main sense; the thing itself and not what is around it — after the noun
examples: The city proper has about 600,000 people, but the metro area has two million.
We didn't reach the town proper until noon.
The meeting proper doesn't start until ten.

senses.head: Belonging to or typical of a particular person, thing or place — formal, in proper to
examples: The judge acted within the powers proper to her office.
They studied the plants proper to the desert Southwest.

senses.head: In grammar, naming one particular person, place or thing — in proper noun, proper name
examples: Chicago is a proper noun, so it starts with a capital letter.
Most proper names don't take the.

entries.position: both — before a noun = right, suitable (the proper tools); right after the noun = in the strict sense, the thing itself (the city proper)
entries.comparison: more/most — in the polite sense: more proper, most proper
entries.takes: for + noun = suitable for (proper for a wedding); to + noun = belonging to (formal: customs proper to the region); it is proper to / that
entries.contrast: Position changes the meaning. Before the noun proper = correct, suitable: the proper place (подходящее место). Right after the noun = strictly speaking, the thing itself: the city proper (собственно город, без пригородов), the concert proper (сам концерт, без разогрева). Russian собственный (own) is not proper: my own room, not my proper room. British a proper mess (= total) is not American; Americans say a real mess. The adverb is properly: Do it properly, not Do it proper.

examples: The new model is available in three colors.
We booked the only room available.
Fresh seafood is more widely available on the coast.
Is Dr. Lee available on Thursday afternoon?
The senator was not available for comment.
I'm available to help after five.
Is he available, or is he seeing someone?
All the available guys at the party were ten years younger than me.
Her father was never emotionally available to her.
After the divorce, he wasn't emotionally available to anyone.

senses.head: Able to be bought, used or got
examples: The new model is available in three colors.
We booked the only room available.
Fresh seafood is more widely available on the coast.

senses.head: Of a person: free to meet, talk or do something; not busy
examples: Is Dr. Lee available on Thursday afternoon?
The senator was not available for comment.
I'm available to help after five.

senses.head: Not in a romantic relationship, and so free to start one
examples: Is he available, or is he seeing someone?
All the available guys at the party were ten years younger than me.

senses.head: Able and willing to share your feelings and give emotional support — often emotionally available
examples: Her father was never emotionally available to her.
After the divorce, he wasn't emotionally available to anyone.

entries.position: both — also right after the noun, especially after a superlative, only or every: the best seats available, the only room available
entries.comparison: more/most — more available, most available, usually with an adverb: more widely available
entries.takes: to + person or group (available to all members); for + noun (available for comment, available for rent); to-infinitive (available to help)
entries.contrast: After the noun, available follows a superlative, the only or every: the cheapest flight available, every seat available; the available seats is also fine. With a person it means free, not busy: Are you available Thursday? = Are you free Thursday? Russian доступный is not always available: доступные цены are affordable prices, доступное объяснение is an accessible or easy-to-understand explanation, and a building open to wheelchairs is accessible.

examples: Is it possible to get there by train?
Thanks to donors, the new library was made possible.
The doctors did everything possible to save him.
It's possible that she just forgot.
Thunderstorms are possible later tonight.
There's another possible explanation.
We want the best possible result for our clients.
Please reply as soon as possible.
It happened at the worst time possible.
She's being talked about as a possible candidate for mayor.
We looked at three possible locations for the new store.

senses.head: Able to be done or achieved
examples: Is it possible to get there by train?
Thanks to donors, the new library was made possible.
The doctors did everything possible to save him.

senses.head: That may happen or be true, but is not certain
examples: It's possible that she just forgot.
Thunderstorms are possible later tonight.
There's another possible explanation.

senses.head: The most or least that can exist or be done — used with superlatives and with as … as
examples: We want the best possible result for our clients.
Please reply as soon as possible.
It happened at the worst time possible.

senses.head: Suitable for a purpose, and so worth considering or choosing
examples: She's being talked about as a possible candidate for mayor.
We looked at three possible locations for the new store.

entries.type: evaluative — whether something can happen or be done
entries.position: both — also right after the noun, especially after a superlative or every, all, only: the lowest price possible = the lowest possible price
entries.comparison: not gradable — but it often strengthens a superlative: the best possible, as soon as possible
entries.takes: to-infinitive after it (It's possible to park here); for + person + to-infinitive (possible for us to meet); that-clause after it (It's possible that she forgot)
entries.contrast: With a to-infinitive, the subject of possible is it, never the person: It's possible for me to come or I can come, not I am possible to come. After the noun it follows a superlative or every/all: the best result possible and the best possible result are both right; every effort possible = every possible effort. possible = может быть; likely or probable = скорее всего. Russian Возможно, он прав is Maybe he's right or He may be right, not Possible he is right. The adverb is possibly: Could you possibly help?

examples: The shop sells ice cream in every flavor imaginable.
It was the worst weather imaginable for a wedding.
We tried every imaginable way to fix it.
Is a world without cars even imaginable?
Twenty years ago, a phone like this was hardly imaginable.

senses.head: Used after a superlative or every, all, no to say that something includes everything or is the most that can be thought of
examples: The shop sells ice cream in every flavor imaginable.
It was the worst weather imaginable for a wedding.
We tried every imaginable way to fix it.

senses.head: Possible to imagine or think of
examples: Is a world without cars even imaginable?
Twenty years ago, a phone like this was hardly imaginable.

entries.type: emphasizing — strengthens a superlative or every, all, no
entries.position: both — before a noun (every imaginable color) and after be (Is it even imaginable?); also right after the noun, usually after a superlative or every, all, no: every color imaginable
entries.contrast: imaginable mostly strengthens a superlative or every/all/no, and then it sits naturally after the noun: the best food imaginable (лучшая еда, какую только можно представить), every problem imaginable (все мыслимые проблемы). Don't confuse it with imaginary = not real (an imaginary friend, воображаемый друг) or imaginative = full of new ideas (an imaginative writer, писатель с богатым воображением).

examples: The president-elect will take office on January 20.
She met with the mayor-elect on Tuesday.
The governor-elect named her new chief of staff.
The preacher warned that only the elect few would be saved.
The Puritans saw themselves as an elect people.

senses.head: Chosen in an election but not yet in office — after a title
examples: The president-elect will take office on January 20.
She met with the mayor-elect on Tuesday.
The governor-elect named her new chief of staff.

senses.head: Specially chosen or selected, especially by God — formal or religious, before the noun
examples: The preacher warned that only the elect few would be saved.
The Puritans saw themselves as an elect people.

entries.русский: избранный (но ещё не вступивший в должность)
entries.position: after the noun — joined to a title, usually with a hyphen: the president-elect, the governor-elect; before the noun only in the formal chosen sense (the elect few)
entries.form: joined to a title with a hyphen; plural on the title: presidents-elect
entries.contrast: The adjective elect comes after a title: the president-elect (избранный президент, ещё не вступивший в должность), not the elect president. Once the person takes office, the title stands alone: the president. For someone already in office, Russian избранный is elected: the newly elected mayor, an elected official. to elect is the verb (They elected her mayor); the elect is a noun (избранные).

entries.meaning: In large numbers or amounts; plenty. ---
examples: The outlet mall has bargains galore this weekend.
There were prizes galore for the kids.
The movie has car chases and explosions galore.
entries.position: after the noun — only: bargains galore, never galore bargains or The bargains were galore
entries.contrast: galore comes only after the noun, and the noun is plural or uncountable: restaurants galore (ресторанов хоть отбавляй), fun galore. It never goes before the noun and never after be: not galore restaurants, not The restaurants are galore. It is informal and cheerful, common in ads; in neutral writing use plenty of or lots of.

entries.meaning: In large amounts; more than enough. ---
examples: There was food aplenty at the church picnic.
The team has talent aplenty but no real leader.
In a good summer, there are tomatoes aplenty.
entries.position: after the noun — mainly (food aplenty); sometimes after be in literary style
entries.contrast: aplenty goes after the noun, like galore: food aplenty (еды вдоволь), not aplenty food. It sounds literary or journalistic; in speech Americans say plenty of food or lots of food. plenty comes before of + noun; aplenty comes after the noun, with no of.

examples: To the kids, the new principal was evil incarnate.
In the movie he plays the devil incarnate.
She was elegance incarnate in that black dress.
Christians believe that Jesus is God incarnate.
In the story, a god incarnate walks among ordinary people.

senses.head: Being the perfect or most extreme example of a quality, as if it had a human body
examples: To the kids, the new principal was evil incarnate.
In the movie he plays the devil incarnate.
She was elegance incarnate in that black dress.

senses.head: In human form; having a human body — religious
examples: Christians believe that Jesus is God incarnate.
In the story, a god incarnate walks among ordinary people.

entries.position: after the noun — evil incarnate, the devil incarnate
entries.contrast: incarnate goes after the noun, usually an abstract noun with no article: evil incarnate, greed incarnate (воплощённое зло, сама жадность). Not incarnate evil. The adjective ends in a weak -nuht; the rare verb to incarnate ends in -nayt. In everyday American English, personified or the embodiment of is more common: She is kindness personified.

examples: It soon became apparent that we were lost.
The dog started barking for no apparent reason.
The problems became more apparent as the year went on.
Police say the death was an apparent suicide.
Despite her apparent calm, she was terrified.
The apparent winner lost after a recount.
The prince is heir apparent to the throne.
She's seen as the heir apparent to the current CEO.

senses.head: Easy to see or understand; obvious — usually after a verb
examples: It soon became apparent that we were lost.
The dog started barking for no apparent reason.
The problems became more apparent as the year went on.

senses.head: Seeming to be true or real, although it may not be — before the noun
examples: Police say the death was an apparent suicide.
Despite her apparent calm, she was terrified.
The apparent winner lost after a recount.

senses.head: Certain to take a title or position in the future — in heir apparent, after the noun
examples: The prince is heir apparent to the throne.
She's seen as the heir apparent to the current CEO.

entries.position: both — after be = clear, obvious (It was apparent that…); before a noun often = seeming (his apparent calm); after heir = next in line (the heir apparent)
entries.takes: to + person (apparent to everyone); from + noun (apparent from her face); that-clause after it (It was apparent that he was lying)
entries.contrast: Position shifts the meaning. After be, and in it is apparent that, apparent = obvious (очевидный). Before the noun it usually means seeming, and the truth may be different: his apparent success (кажущийся успех), an apparent heart attack (судя по всему, сердечный приступ). for no apparent reason = for no visible reason. The adverb apparently follows the second meaning: Apparently he quit = I heard he quit (похоже, говорят), not Obviously he quit. After heir it follows the noun: the heir apparent.

examples: Are you certain you locked the door?
I'm not certain of the exact date.
I've never been more certain of anything in my life.
The bill is certain to pass the Senate.
It's certain that prices will go up next year.
Without a helmet, he faced certain death.
Certain foods can trigger migraines.
The store is closed on certain holidays.
You have to be a certain age to rent a car.
A certain Mr. Jones called while you were out.
The letter was signed by a certain Dr. Alvarez.
To a certain extent, she's right.
The old house has a certain charm.
There's always a certain amount of risk.

senses.head: Completely sure; having no doubt — after a verb
examples: Are you certain you locked the door?
I'm not certain of the exact date.
I've never been more certain of anything in my life.

senses.head: Sure to happen or be true; definite
examples: The bill is certain to pass the Senate.
It's certain that prices will go up next year.
Without a helmet, he faced certain death.

senses.head: Particular, but not named or described exactly — before the noun
examples: Certain foods can trigger migraines.
The store is closed on certain holidays.
You have to be a certain age to rent a car.

senses.head: In a certain + name: a person the listener doesn't know, known only by that name
examples: A certain Mr. Jones called while you were out.
The letter was signed by a certain Dr. Alvarez.

senses.head: Some, but not a large amount; real but hard to describe exactly — in a certain
examples: To a certain extent, she's right.
The old house has a certain charm.
There's always a certain amount of risk.

entries.position: both — after be = sure (I'm certain); before a noun = definite (certain death) or particular, some (certain people, a certain Mr. Jones)
entries.comparison: more/most — in the sure senses only: more certain, most certain
entries.takes: of or about + noun or -ing (certain of the facts); that-clause (certain that she's right); to-infinitive = sure to happen (She's certain to win)
entries.contrast: Position and article change the meaning. After be certain = sure: I'm certain (я уверен). Before a noun without an article it can mean sure to happen, certain death (верная смерть), or some, not named, certain people (некоторые люди). a certain = one particular: a certain Mr. Smith (некий мистер Смит), a certain charm (некоторое обаяние). She is certain to win = she will surely win; She is certain that she'll win = she believes it. When Russian определённый means exact, use specific: a specific date.

examples: Is there a particular book you're looking for?
I love that particular shade of blue.
He left for no particular reason.
Pay particular attention to the last question.
This is a matter of particular importance to veterans.
He's very particular about how his coffee is made.
My cat is particular about what she eats.
She's more particular about hotels than I am.
It's a style of cooking particular to southern Louisiana.
The problem isn't particular to our school; every district has it.

senses.head: Used to show that you mean one specific person or thing and not others
examples: Is there a particular book you're looking for?
I love that particular shade of blue.
He left for no particular reason.

senses.head: Greater than usual; special
examples: Pay particular attention to the last question.
This is a matter of particular importance to veterans.

senses.head: Very careful to choose only what you like, and hard to please; fussy
examples: He's very particular about how his coffee is made.
My cat is particular about what she eats.
She's more particular about hotels than I am.

senses.head: Belonging to or found in only one person, place or thing — in particular to
examples: It's a style of cooking particular to southern Louisiana.
The problem isn't particular to our school; every district has it.

entries.type: classifying — this one and not another; also quality (fussy)
entries.position: both — before a noun = specific or special (this particular case); after be = fussy (She's particular about food); after the noun with to = found only in (a dish particular to Louisiana)
entries.comparison: more/most — in the fussy sense only: more particular, most particular
entries.takes: about + noun or -ing = fussy (particular about his coffee); to + noun = found only in (particular to the region)
entries.contrast: Position changes the meaning. Before the noun particular = this specific one: a particular hotel (определённый, конкретный отель), or special: of particular importance (особой важности). After be, about a person, it = fussy: She's very particular (очень разборчивая). After the noun with to = found only in: a custom particular to New Orleans (свойственный). Russian частный is usually private (a private school) or individual; частный случай is a special case. in particular (в частности, особенно) is a fixed phrase.

Poor Sam — he's been sick all week.
The poor dog was shaking in the rain.
Oh, you poor thing!
I've always been a poor swimmer.
He's a poor judge of character.
She's poor at keeping in touch with old friends.
Diets poor in fiber can cause health problems.
The soil here is poor, so not much grows.
It's a country poor in natural resources.

senses.head: Having very little money and few possessions
examples: They grew up poor in rural Mississippi.
It's one of the poorest counties in the country.
The program helps poor families pay for heat.

senses.head: Not good enough in quality, amount or condition; bad
examples: The food was great, but the service was poor.
My grandfather is in poor health.
Poor sales forced the store to close.

senses.head: Deserving pity; unlucky — before the noun only
examples: Poor Sam — he's been sick all week.
The poor dog was shaking in the rain.
Oh, you poor thing!

senses.head: Not skilled or not good at doing something
examples: I've always been a poor swimmer.
He's a poor judge of character.
She's poor at keeping in touch with old friends.

senses.head: Having very little of something that is needed — often after the noun, in poor in
examples: Diets poor in fiber can cause health problems.
The soil here is poor, so not much grows.
It's a country poor in natural resources.

entries.position: both — before a noun can mean to be pitied (the poor guy); after be never to be pitied, only without money, of low quality or lacking (They're poor, The service was poor); after the noun with in = lacking (food poor in vitamins)
entries.takes: in + noun = lacking (poor in natural resources); at + noun or -ing = bad at (poor at math)
entries.contrast: Before the noun poor often means unlucky, to be pitied, with nothing to do with money: the poor woman can be бедняжка. After be it never means that: The woman is poor = у неё нет денег. After the noun with in = lacking: a diet poor in fiber. the poor = poor people (plural verb, no -s): The poor pay more. For low quality, poor is the natural word with health, results and performance: poor health, poor grades. In many American accents poor sounds like pour.
